claims.text: Deformation at intermediate temperatures induces rapid, localized nanoclustering at grain boundaries in initially single-phase CrMnFeCoNi.
The grain-boundary nanoclusters consist of separately clustered principal elements including Cr, Ni, and Mn.
Nanoclustering of Cr, Ni, and Mn at grain boundaries reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion promotes crack initiation along grain boundaries.
Intermediate-temperature deformation of CrMnFeCoNi produces ductility loss correlated with grain-boundary cracking.
Nanoclustering causes a transition from ductile to brittle failure and a degradation of toughness.
The proposed embrittlement mechanism is distinct from the mechanisms operating in conventional alloys.
The initial CrMnFeCoNi alloy is single-phase and FCC.
The initial alloy has no pre-existing grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitates.
Room-temperature testing is a condition under which no dynamic nanosegregation is expected.
Complex interactions among multiple principal elements facilitate rapid and selective grain-boundary segregation.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion prevents dislocations from effectively blunting cracks.
Intermediate-temperature samples will show more intergranular cracking than the initial or room-temperature state.
Intermediate-temperature samples will exhibit reduced tensile ductility.
Intermediate-temperature nanoclustering will lower impact toughness or fracture toughness.
A microalloying addition can inhibit fast grain-boundary nanocluster formation while retaining the intended single-phase alloy state.
Suppressing grain-boundary nanoclustering will preserve higher toughness relative to the non-microalloyed alloy.
Grain-boundary nanoclustering can be detected using atom probe tomography.
At extreme high temperatures, oxidation rather than nanoclustering will dominate the alloy response.
The proposed mechanism may vary across different HEA compositions because the relevant elemental combinations differ.
